claim: Haploinsufficiency for GATA6 is associated with congenital heart disease (CHD) with variable comorbidity of pancreatic or diaphragm defects.
source: Haploinsufficiency for GATA6 is associated with congenital heart disease (CHD) with variable comorbidity of pancreatic or diaphragm defects, although the etiology of disease is not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established association, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: GATA6 loss-of-function hESCs had a profound impairment in cardiac progenitor cell (CPC) specification and cardiomyocyte (CM) generation.
source: GATA6 loss-of-function hESCs had a profound impairment in cardiac progenitor cell (CPC) specification and cardiomyocyte (CM) generation due to early defects during the mesendoderm and lateral mesoderm patterning stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including flow cytometry and RT-qPCR results.

claim: GATA6 loss-of-function causes early defects during the mesendoderm and lateral mesoderm patterning stages.
source: GATA6 loss-of-function hESCs had a profound impairment in cardiac progenitor cell (CPC) specification and cardiomyocyte (CM) generation due to early defects during the mesendoderm and lateral mesoderm patterning stages.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and flow cytometry analysis at early differentiation time points.

claim: GATA6 regulates genes of the WNT and BMP programs during early mesoderm patterning.
source: Profiling by RNA-seq and CUT&RUN identified genes of the WNT and BMP programs regulated by GATA6 during early mesoderm patterning.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and CUT&RUN sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GATA6 binds with developmental transcription factors and chromatin remodelers.
source: Furthermore, interactome analysis detected GATA6 binding with developmental transcription factors and chromatin remodelers, suggesting cooperative regulation of cardiac lineage gene accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GATA6 cooperatively regulates cardiac lineage gene accessibility with developmental transcription factors and chromatin remodelers.
source: Furthermore, interactome analysis detected GATA6 binding with developmental transcription factors and chromatin remodelers, suggesting cooperative regulation of cardiac lineage gene accessibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the RIME data showing protein interactions, though direct functional evidence of cooperative regulation is speculative.

claim: Modulating WNT and BMP inputs during the first 48 hr of cardiac differentiation partially rescues CPC and CM defects in GATA6 heterozygous and homozygous mutant hESCs.
source: We show that modulating WNT and BMP inputs during the first 48 hr of cardiac differentiation is sufficient to partially rescue CPC and CM defects in GATA6 heterozygous and homozygous mutant hESCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of cardiac differentiation defects with CHIR and reduced BMP4 treatment.

claim: CHD is the most common human birth defect, affecting nearly 1% of live births.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common human birth defect, affecting nearly 1% of live births (Hoffman and Kaplan, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CHD is generally understood to derive from dysfunction in the growth, morphogenesis, and/or differentiation of cardiac-fated progenitor cell derivatives.
source: CHD is generally understood to derive from dysfunction in the growth, morphogenesis, and/or differentiation of cardiac-fated progenitor cell derivatives; however, the genetic and molecular networks governing these processes remain under investigation.
evidence: This represents established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Treatment options for CHD are limited to surgical interventions that can save the life of the infant but do not correct the underlying genetics.
source: Treatment options are limited to surgical interventions that can save the life of the infant but do not correct the underlying genetics.
evidence: This represents current clinical practice and knowledge in the field.

claim: Causative genetic variants in CHD may contribute to complications and morbidity in adulthood.
source: The causative genetic variants may contribute to complications and morbidity in adulthood (Woudstra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GATA factors are named by their ability to bind to the consensus sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G).
source: GATA factors, named by their ability to bind to the consensus sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G) (Patient and McGhee, 2002), represent six family members with GATA4/5/6 expressed in the developing heart of early-stage embryos (Peterkin et al., 2007; Molkentin, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GATA4/5/6 are expressed in the developing heart of early-stage embryos.
source: GATA factors, named by their ability to bind to the consensus sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G) (Patient and McGhee, 2002), represent six family members with GATA4/5/6 expressed in the developing heart of early-stage embryos (Peterkin et al., 2007; Molkentin, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GATA4/5/6 transcription factors regulate multiple stages of heart development including the specification, proliferation, and differentiation of cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs).
source: GATA4/5/6 transcription factors regulate multiple stages of heart development including the specification, proliferation, and differentiation of cardiac progenitor cells (CPCs) (Peterkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GATA6 knockout (KO) mice exhibit early embryonic arrest during primitive streak formation due to defects in visceral endoderm.
source: Notably, GATA6 knockout (KO) mice exhibit early embryonic arrest during primitive streak formation due to defects in visceral endoderm, a phenotype that has complicated the study of the early developmental function of GATA6 in vivo (Morrisey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mice with conditional deletion of GATA6 from early CPCs develop heart abnormalities including atrioventricular canal defects, ventricular septal defects, and partial loss of trabeculae.
source: Mice with conditional deletion of GATA6 from early CPCs develop heart abnormalities including atrioventricular canal defects, ventricular septal defects, and partial loss of trabeculae (Tian et al., 2010; van Berlo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GATA6 conditional homozygous KO mice die at birth due to heart malformations.
source: While these GATA6 conditional homozygous KO mice die at birth due to heart malformations, few cardiac phenotypes were reported in the GATA6 heterozygous mutants, except for recent reports of bicuspid aortic valve and heart rhythm abnormalities (Gharibeh et al., 2018; Gharibeh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Few cardiac phenotypes were reported in GATA6 heterozygous mutant mice, except for recent reports of bicuspid aortic valve and heart rhythm abnormalities.
source: While these GATA6 conditional homozygous KO mice die at birth due to heart malformations, few cardiac phenotypes were reported in the GATA6 heterozygous mutants, except for recent reports of bicuspid aortic valve and heart rhythm abnormalities (Gharibeh et al., 2018; Gharibeh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In humans, heterozygous mutations in GATA6 are associated with various forms of CHD including outflow tract (OFT) defects, septal defects, and Tetralogy of Fallot.
source: In humans, heterozygous mutations in GATA6 are associated with various forms of CHD including outflow tract (OFT) defects, septal defects, and Tetralogy of Fallot (Wang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GATA6 is required for the development of multiple mesoderm and endoderm-derived organs.
source: GATA6 is required for the development of multiple mesoderm and endoderm-derived organs, and some CHD patients with heterozygous GATA6 mutations have comorbidities including pancreatic agenesis, neonatal diabetes, or congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Gong et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some CHD patients with heterozygous GATA6 mutations have comorbidities including pancreatic agenesis, neonatal diabetes, or congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
source: GATA6 is required for the development of multiple mesoderm and endoderm-derived organs, and some CHD patients with heterozygous GATA6 mutations have comorbidities including pancreatic agenesis, neonatal diabetes, or congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Gong et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The phenotypic diversity of birth defects in patients containing GATA6 mutations illustrates the complexity of human haploinsufficiency.
source: The phenotypic diversity of birth defects in patients containing GATA6 mutations illustrates the complexity of human haploinsufficiency; there is likely a combination of variants in modifying or interacting genes that converge to influence the disease phenotype (Fahed et al., 2013; Seidman and Seidman, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is likely a combination of variants in modifying or interacting genes that converge to influence the disease phenotype in GATA6 haploinsufficiency.
source: The phenotypic diversity of birth defects in patients containing GATA6 mutations illustrates the complexity of human haploinsufficiency; there is likely a combination of variants in modifying or interacting genes that converge to influence the disease phenotype (Fahed et al., 2013; Seidman and Seidman, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Previous studies of the function of GATA6 in model organisms have not sufficiently modeled the variety of cardiac (and noncardiac) defects observed in humans.
source: Previous studies of the function of GATA6 in model organisms have not sufficiently modeled the variety of cardiac (and noncardiac) defects observed in humans and most describe phenotypes only after homozygous inactivation of the gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing literature.

claim: Most previous studies of GATA6 in model organisms describe phenotypes only after homozygous inactivation of the gene.
source: Previous studies of the function of GATA6 in model organisms have not sufficiently modeled the variety of cardiac (and noncardiac) defects observed in humans and most describe phenotypes only after homozygous inactivation of the gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing literature.

claim: Species-specific functions for GATA6 may differ between mouse and humans.
source: Species-specific functions for GATA6 may differ between mouse and humans, for example, raising the question of how observations made in model organisms relate to human cardiac development.
evidence: This is a speculative statement raising a research question.

claim: Current in vitro cardiac-directed differentiation protocols for human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provide powerful tools for studying the transcriptional regulatory networks relevant to CHD.
source: Current in vitro cardiac-directed differentiation protocols for human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provide powerful tools for studying the transcriptional regulatory networks relevant to CHD (Mummery et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A previous study using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) with CRISPR-Cas9-induced GATA6 mutations showed that GATA6 is required at the stages of CPC and cardiomyocyte (CM) differentiation.
source: A previous study using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) with CRISPR-Cas9-induced GATA6 mutations showed that GATA6 is required at the stages of CPC and cardiomyocyte (CM) differentiation (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GATA6 is required for definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation toward the pancreatic lineage.
source: GATA6 is also required for definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation toward the pancreatic lineage as reported in several studies using hPSCs (Shi et al., 2017; Heslop et al., 2021; Chia et al., 2019; Tiyaboonchai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The function of GATA6 during early mesoderm patterning of human cardiac differentiation has not been explored.
source: However, the function of GATA6 during early mesoderm patterning of human cardiac differentiation has not been explored, and how in vitro cardiac and DE lineage phenotypes caused by GATA6 loss-of-function relate to one another is not understood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing literature.

claim: How in vitro cardiac and DE lineage phenotypes caused by GATA6 loss-of-function relate to one another is not understood.
source: However, the function of GATA6 during early mesoderm patterning of human cardiac differentiation has not been explored, and how in vitro cardiac and DE lineage phenotypes caused by GATA6 loss-of-function relate to one another is not understood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing literature.

claim: GATA6-/- cells failed to generate beating CMs and yielded close to 0% cTnT+ CMs when examined by flow cytometry.
source: GATA6-/- cells failed to generate beating CMs and yielded close to 0% cTnT+ CMs when examined by flow cytometry (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: GATA6+/- hESCs generated beating CMs (~25% cTnT+) but at a significantly reduced efficiency compared to WT cells (~55% cTnT+).
source: In contrast, GATA6+/- hESCs did generate beating CMs (~25% cTnT+) but at a significantly reduced efficiency compared to WT cells (~55% cTnT+, Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: GATA6+/- CMs obtained were comparable morphologically to WT CMs with no obvious sarcomere defects.
source: GATA6+/- CMs obtained were comparable morphologically to WT CMs with no obvious sarcomere defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No significant differences in %cTnT+ were observed between clones of the same genotype.
source: No significant differences in %cTnT+ were observed between clones of the same genotype (Figure 1C); therefore, data from lines with the same genotypes were combined in all subsequent comparisons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CPC marker expression levels were significantly reduced in GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- cells relative to WT controls at day 6 of cardiac differentiation.
source: CPC marker expression levels were significantly reduced in GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- cells relative to WT controls, indicating a defect in CPC specification (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At day 6 of cardiac differentiation, there was a clear trend but not a statistically significant difference in the expression levels of CPC markers comparing the GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- genotypes.
source: At this time point there was a clear trend but not a statistically significant difference in the expression levels of CPC markers comparing the GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- genotypes.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of RT-qPCR data.

claim: ISL1 and SMARCD3 expression levels were significantly lower in GATA6+/- cells at day 6 of cardiac differentiation.
source: All were significantly depleted in the GATA6-/- cells, while both ISL1 and SMARCD3 (but not HAND1) levels were significantly lower in the GATA6+/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HAND1 expression levels were not significantly lower in GATA6+/- cells at day 6 of cardiac differentiation.
source: All were significantly depleted in the GATA6-/- cells, while both ISL1 and SMARCD3 (but not HAND1) levels were significantly lower in the GATA6+/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CPC marker expression level was increased (although not to WT levels) in GATA6+/- cells at later stages (days 8–11).
source: We note that an RT-qPCR time course showed that CPC marker expression level was increased (although not to WT levels) in GATA6+/- cells at later stages (days 8–11) while GATA6-/- CPC gene expression levels remained 'flat' in comparison with no increase over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: GATA6-/- CPC gene expression levels remained 'flat' with no increase over time from days 8-11.
source: We note that an RT-qPCR time course showed that CPC marker expression level was increased (although not to WT levels) in GATA6+/- cells at later stages (days 8–11) while GATA6-/- CPC gene expression levels remained 'flat' in comparison with no increase over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The CHIR protocol was overall suboptimal for cardiac differentiation using the H1-hESCs due to substantial variation in CM differentiation efficiency and the occasional failure to generate CMs in WT H1-hESCs.
source: The CHIR protocol was overall suboptimal for cardiac differentiation using the H1-hESCs due to substantial variation in CM differentiation efficiency and the occasional failure to generate CMs in WT H1-hESCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during protocol optimization.

claim: The same phenotype in GATA6-/- cells and GATA6+/- cells was observed using the CHIR protocol as with the cytokine-based protocol.
source: Nevertheless, in successful experiments performed using the CHIR protocol we observed the same phenotype in GATA6-/- cells and GATA6+/- cells using the CHIR protocol as with the cytokine-based protocol (data not shown), consistent with a previous report (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to published literature.

claim: GATA6-/- cells had strongly reduced expression levels of cardiac development-related gene sets including 'OFT septum morphogenesis' and 'heart development' compared to WT controls at day 5 using the CHIR protocol.
source: Differential gene expression and gene ontology (GO) analyses revealed that GATA6-/- cells had strongly reduced expression levels of cardiac development-related gene sets including 'OFT septum morphogenesis' and 'heart development' compared to WT controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: GATA6+/- cells had relatively higher expression levels for many cardiac development genes compared to GATA6-/- cells, but numerous CPC regulatory genes showed decreased levels compared to WT controls.
source: Furthermore, while GATA6+/- cells had relatively higher expression levels for many of these genes compared to GATA6-/- cells, numerous CPC regulatory genes showed decreased levels compared to WT controls (including NKX2.5, TBX20, TBX5, MEF2C, and HAND2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), confirming an impairment of CPC development in differentiating GATA6 mutant hESCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Gene sets related to retinoic acid (RA) signaling were significantly increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT at day 5 using the CHIR protocol.
source: Notably, gene sets related to retinoic acid (RA) signaling were significantly increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), and ALDH1A2 expression (the main enzyme that generates RA) was increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT from days 4–6 using the cytokine-based protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), consistent with a previous study of cardiac differentiation using GATA6 loss-of-function hiPSCs (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F, along with a citation.

claim: ALDH1A2 expression was increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT from days 4–6 using the cytokine-based protocol.
source: Notably, gene sets related to retinoic acid (RA) signaling were significantly increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), and ALDH1A2 expression (the main enzyme that generates RA) was increased in GATA6-/- cells relative to WT from days 4–6 using the cytokine-based protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), consistent with a previous study of cardiac differentiation using GATA6 loss-of-function hiPSCs (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Proper RA signaling is crucial for cardiogenesis including OFT development and cardiac chamber morphogenesis.
source: Proper RA signaling is crucial for cardiogenesis including OFT development and cardiac chamber morphogenesis (Perl and Waxman, 2019), and inhibiting excessive RA signaling in GATA6 mutant hiPSCs was shown to partially rescue CPC marker expression (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inhibiting excessive RA signaling in GATA6 mutant hiPSCs was shown to partially rescue CPC marker expression.
source: Proper RA signaling is crucial for cardiogenesis including OFT development and cardiac chamber morphogenesis (Perl and Waxman, 2019), and inhibiting excessive RA signaling in GATA6 mutant hiPSCs was shown to partially rescue CPC marker expression (Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Upregulated RA signaling in GATA6-/- hESCs during the CPC developmental stage may partially underlie the CM differentiation defects.
source: Thus, upregulated RA signaling in GATA6-/- hESCs during the CPC developmental stage may partially underlie the CM differentiation defects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data and cited literature.

claim: The earliest (and highest) expression level for GATA6 occurs at day 2 of differentiation.
source: Examining protein expression at multiple stages during cardiac differentiation revealed the earliest (and highest) expression level for GATA6 at day 2 of differentiation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At day 3, there was no significant difference in the %K+P+ cells between genotypes (~45% K+P+).
source: At day 3, there was no significant difference in the %K+P+ cells between genotypes (~45% K+P+), but by day 5 the %K+P+ increased to ~72% in WT and GATA6+/- cells, while the %K+P+ was markedly reduced in GATA6-/- cells (~22%, Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: By day 5 the %K+P+ increased to ~72% in WT and GATA6+/- cells, while the %K+P+ was markedly reduced in GATA6-/- cells (~22%).
source: At day 3, there was no significant difference in the %K+P+ cells between genotypes (~45% K+P+), but by day 5 the %K+P+ increased to ~72% in WT and GATA6+/- cells, while the %K+P+ was markedly reduced in GATA6-/- cells (~22%, Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Day 5 sorted K+P+ cells give rise predominantly to CMs.
source: This is consistent with previous reports where sorting and reseeding K+P+ cells at day 3 of cardiac differentiation generated both mesenchymal cells and CMs but day 5 sorted K+P+ cells gave rise predominantly to CMs, indicating that day 5 KP expression is relatively enriched for precardiac mesoderm (Kattman et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Day 5 KP expression is relatively enriched for precardiac mesoderm.
source: This is consistent with previous reports where sorting and reseeding K+P+ cells at day 3 of cardiac differentiation generated both mesenchymal cells and CMs but day 5 sorted K+P+ cells gave rise predominantly to CMs, indicating that day 5 KP expression is relatively enriched for precardiac mesoderm (Kattman et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and inference from the data.

claim: GATA6+/- cells had a small but significant decrease in the %K+P+ cells at day 4 relative to WT.
source: GATA6+/- cells had a small but significant decrease in the %K+P+ cells at day 4 relative to WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that the developing K+P+ cardiac mesoderm in GATA6+/- cells is temporarily defective or delayed relative to WT controls.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The developing K+P+ cardiac mesoderm in GATA6+/- cells is temporarily defective or delayed relative to WT controls.
source: GATA6+/- cells had a small but significant decrease in the %K+P+ cells at day 4 relative to WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that the developing K+P+ cardiac mesoderm in GATA6+/- cells is temporarily defective or delayed relative to WT controls.
evidence: This is an inference based on flow cytometry data.

claim: The decreased %K+P+ observed at day 4 (GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- cells) and day 5 (GATA6-/- cells) relative to WT cells was due to reduced KDR but not PDGFRα expression.
source: Notably, the decreased %K+P+ observed at day 4 (GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- cells) and day 5 (GATA6-/- cells) relative to WT cells was due to reduced KDR but not PDGFRα expression (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that KDR is (directly or indirectly) regulated by GATA6 during cardiac mesoderm patterning.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: KDR is (directly or indirectly) regulated by GATA6 during cardiac mesoderm patterning.
source: Notably, the decreased %K+P+ observed at day 4 (GATA6+/- and GATA6-/- cells) and day 5 (GATA6-/- cells) relative to WT cells was due to reduced KDR but not PDGFRα expression (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating that KDR is (directly or indirectly) regulated by GATA6 during cardiac mesoderm patterning.
evidence: This is an inference based on flow cytometry data.

claim: There was no significant difference in abundance of BRACHYURY+ cells between genotypes at day 2 or 3 of cardiac differentiation.
source: Flow cytometry performed on WT, GATA6+/-, or GATA6-/- cells at day 2 or 3 of cardiac differentiation revealed no significant difference in abundance of BRACHYURY+ cells between genotypes (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: There was no significant change in transcript levels for T or the mesendoderm marker EOMES, or mesoderm markers MESP1, or MESP2 at day 2.
source: Likewise, there was no significant change in transcript levels for T or the mesendoderm marker EOMES, or mesoderm markers MESP1, or MESP2 at day 2 when assessed by RT-qPCR (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: GATA6 mutant hESCs have the capacity to differentiate into a nascent mesendoderm/early mesoderm population that is deficient in patterning cardiac mesoderm.
source: These results indicate that GATA6 mutant hESCs have the capacity to differentiate into a nascent mesendoderm/early mesoderm population that is deficient in patterning cardiac mesoderm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flow cytometry and RT-qPCR data.

claim: Sequentially lineage-restrictive mesodermal cell populations emerge along a developmental trajectory involving primitive streak to lateral mesoderm formation, followed by cardiac mesoderm patterning during gastrulation.
source: During gastrulation, sequentially lineage-restrictive mesodermal cell populations emerge along a developmental trajectory involving primitive streak to lateral mesoderm formation, followed by cardiac mesoderm patterning (Miquerol and Kelly, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GATA6 is required during the earliest stages of lateral and precardiac mesoderm patterning.
source: As GATA6 loss-of-function hESCs differentiated to an emergent mesendoderm/mesoderm stage but failed to properly generate cardiac mesdoderm, we hypothesized that GATA6 is required during the earliest stages of lateral and precardiac mesoderm patterning.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: GO analysis of decreased DEGs in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at days 2 and 3 included 'heart development' and 'OFT septum morphogenesis'.
source: GO analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the biological process (BP) subcollection for differentially expressed genes (DEGs; defined as p-adj<0.05 and log2(fold change)>0.5) comparing GATA6-/- to WT samples revealed decreased enrichment for GO terms including 'heart development' (e.g., HAND1) and 'OFT septum morphogenesis' (e.g., NRP1) at days 2 and 3, suggesting a disruption of early cardiac signature genes (Figure 3A, C and D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A, C and D.

claim: The decreased enrichment for the 'OFT septum morphogenesis' GO term is consistent with the conclusions of a previous study of GATA6 mutations in hPSCs in the context of cardiac differentiation.
source: The decreased enrichment for the 'OFT septum morphogenesis' GO term is consistent with the conclusions of a previous study of GATA6 mutations in hPSCs in the context of cardiac differentiation (Sharma et al., 2020); however, the results presented here implicate this program at a much earlier developmental stage (D2 mesendoderm/lateral mesoderm).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and comparison with the current data.

claim: The results presented here implicate the OFT septum morphogenesis program at a much earlier developmental stage (D2 mesendoderm/lateral mesoderm).
source: The decreased enrichment for the 'OFT septum morphogenesis' GO term is consistent with the conclusions of a previous study of GATA6 mutations in hPSCs in the context of cardiac differentiation (Sharma et al., 2020); however, the results presented here implicate this program at a much earlier developmental stage (D2 mesendoderm/lateral mesoderm).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data at day 2.

claim: GO analysis of increased DEGs in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at days 2 and 3 included 'extracellular matrix (ECM) organization', 'skeletal system development', and 'AP axis specification'.
source: Conversely, GO analysis of increased DEGs in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at days 2 and 3 included 'extracellular matrix (ECM) organization', 'skeletal system development', and 'AP axis specification' (Figure 3B and D), suggesting that GATA6-/- cells are biased to other lineages such as paraxial mesoderm or retain an early mesodermal phenotype by day 3.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: GATA6-/- cells are biased to other lineages such as paraxial mesoderm or retain an early mesodermal phenotype by day 3.
source: Conversely, GO analysis of increased DEGs in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at days 2 and 3 included 'extracellular matrix (ECM) organization', 'skeletal system development', and 'AP axis specification' (Figure 3B and D), suggesting that GATA6-/- cells are biased to other lineages such as paraxial mesoderm or retain an early mesodermal phenotype by day 3.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA-seq data.

claim: WNT and BMP-related genes were dysregulated in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at day 2.
source: We observed dysregulation of genes related to the WNT and BMP networks in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at day 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and GO and GSEA revealed decreased levels of 'positive regulation of the BMP pathway' and increased levels of 'negative regulation of canonical WNT pathway' at day 2 or 3 relative to WT (Figure 3A, B, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and Figure 3A, B, D and E.

claim: GO and GSEA revealed decreased levels of 'positive regulation of the BMP pathway' and increased levels of 'negative regulation of canonical WNT pathway' at day 2 or 3 relative to WT.
source: We observed dysregulation of genes related to the WNT and BMP networks in GATA6-/- samples relative to WT at day 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and GO and GSEA revealed decreased levels of 'positive regulation of the BMP pathway' and increased levels of 'negative regulation of canonical WNT pathway' at day 2 or 3 relative to WT (Figure 3A, B, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A, B, D and E.

claim: Several decreased DEGs identified in GATA6-/- cells at day 2 or 3 relative to WT samples included negative regulators of WNT signaling, including SFRP1 and TLE1.
source: Several dDEGs identified in GATA6-/- cells at day 2 or 3 relative to WT samples included negative regulators of WNT signaling, including SFRP1 and TLE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G), and antagonists of the BMP pathway, such as BMPER and SMAD6 (Figure 3A and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G), indicating that the overall transcriptional response induced by the WNT and BMP pathways is dysregulated.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G.

claim: Several decreased DEGs identified in GATA6-/- cells at day 2 or 3 relative to WT samples included antagonists of the BMP pathway, such as BMPER and SMAD6.
source: Several dDEGs identified in GATA6-/- cells at day 2 or 3 relative to WT samples included negative regulators of WNT signaling, including SFRP1 and TLE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G), and antagonists of the BMP pathway, such as BMPER and SMAD6 (Figure 3A and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G), indicating that the overall transcriptional response induced by the WNT and BMP pathways is dysregulated.

claim: GATA6 was shown to interact with EOMES during early DE differentiation.

claim: An interaction between GATA6 and EOMES is similarly necessary during early lateral mesoderm patterning.

claim: GATA6 cooperates with EOMES to co-regulate genes required for lateral mesoderm patterning.

evidence: This is an inference based on GSEA analysis.

claim: 1273 significant differentially bound sites were identified for GATA6 relative to IgG control samples at day 2 of differentiation, associated with 953 transcriptional start sites (TSS) for unique genes.
source: 1273 significant differentially bound sites were identified for GATA6 relative to IgG control samples, associated with 953 transcriptional start sites (TSS) for unique genes (Figure 4A).

source: Significant GATA6 binding sites predominately localized to intronic (46.03%) and distal intergenic (32.21%, >5 kb from TSS) regions (Figure 4A), consistent with previous reports of GATA6 binding distribution (Sulahian et al., 2014; Fisher et al., 2017).

claim: Transcription factor binding motif enrichment analysis revealed the strongest enrichment at GATA6 bound loci for 'GATA' motifs, as well as 'LHX-like' and 'EOMES' motifs.
source: Transcription factor binding motif enrichment analysis revealed the strongest enrichment at GATA6 bound loci for 'GATA' motifs, as well as 'LHX-like' (LIM homeobox transcription factor; expressed in cardiac and other mesodermal derivatives; Costello et al., 2015) and 'EOMES' motifs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GO analysis of the gene list nearby significant GATA6 binding peaks showed striking similarity to GO analysis from RNA-seq decreased DEGs in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT), including 'OFT septum morphogenesis', 'BMP signaling pathway', and 'WNT signaling pathway'.
source: GO analysis of the gene list nearby significant GATA6 binding peaks showed striking similarity to GO analysis from RNA-seq dDEGs in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT), including 'OFT septum morphogenesis', 'BMP signaling pathway', and 'WNT signaling pathway' (Figure 4C).

claim: There was an overlap of CUT&RUN identified genes with day 2 (17.9%) and 3 (16.8%) RNA-seq decreased DEGs in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT) representing high likelihood direct targets of GATA6 including the cardiac development-related genes HAND1 and MYOCD.
source: Additionally, we observed an overlap of CUT&RUN identified genes with day 2 (17.9%) and 3 (16.8%) RNA-seq dDEGs in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT) representing high likelihood direct targets of GATA6 including the cardiac development-related genes HAND1 and MYOCD (Figure 4D).

claim: GATA6 peaks mapped to day 2 and 3 decreased DEGs confirmed binding in intronic regions or at distal intergenic regions that overlapped with known enhancer-like signatures identified by the ENCODE Project.
source: Visualizing the localization of these GATA6 peaks that mapped to day 2 and 3 dDEGs confirmed binding in intronic regions or at distal intergenic regions that overlapped with known enhancer-like signatures identified by the ENCODE Project (Moore et al., 2020; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by genome browser visualization shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GATA6 binding peaks were found in associated putative enhancers for several WNT-related genes such as MCC and LGR5, as well as BMP-related genes including SMAD6.
source: These included several WNT-related genes such as MCC and LGR5, as well as BMP-related genes including SMAD6 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by genome browser visualization shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genes with GATA6 binding peaks in associated putative enhancers are likely to be direct targets for the WNT/BMP networks.
source: In Figure 4F, genes are highlighted in red that have GATA6 binding peaks in associated putative enhancers that are likely to be direct targets for the WNT/BMP networks.

source: These are distinguished from WNT/BMP pathway genes that were not bound by GATA6 yet are downregulated in the GATA6 mutant cells and are more likely to be indirect targets.

claim: Comparing day 2 GATA6 CUT&RUN data, day 2 RNA-seq data, and EOMES CHIP-seq data revealed 32 genes that had triple-overlap.
source: Comparing these datasets revealed 32 genes that had triple-overlap of day 2 GATA6 CUT&RUN identified genes (953 genes nearby significantly bound sites), day 2 RNA-seq dDEGs, and EOMES CHIP-seq targets (Teo et al., 2011; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Among the triple-overlap genes are known cardiac development factors including LGR5 and PRDM1.
source: Among this list of triple-overlap genes are known cardiac development factors including LGR5, which was reported to be required for hESC-CM differentiation (Jha et al., 2017), and PRDM1, which is expressed in the SHF and involved in OFT morphogenesis (Vincent et al., 2014).

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The GATA6 peaks directly overlapped with many EOMES CHIP-seq peaks.
source: Visualizing the location of these triple-overlap genes confirmed that the GATA6 peaks directly overlapped with many EOMES CHIP-seq peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that GATA6 and EOMES interact to co-regulate genes required for precardiac mesoderm patterning.
evidence: This is supported by genome browser visualization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GATA6 and EOMES interact to co-regulate genes required for precardiac mesoderm patterning.

evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of GATA6 and EOMES binding sites.

claim: 99 significant interacting proteins at day 2 and 52 unique proteins at day 4 of cardiac differentiation were identified bound to GATA6 compared to IgG control samples.
source: 99 significant interacting proteins at day 2 and 52 unique proteins at day 4 of cardiac differentiation were identified bound to GATA6 compared to IgG control samples (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: EOMES was one of the most enriched proteins bound to GATA6 at day 2 but was not identified in the day 4 GATA6-RIME analysis.
source: EOMES was one of the most enriched proteins bound to GATA6 at day 2 but was not identified in the day 4 GATA6-RIME analysis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 81.8% of proteins identified by GATA6-RIME at day 2 were not encoded by significantly DEGs identified by day 2 RNA-seq (GATA6-/- vs. WT).
source: 81.8% of proteins identified by GATA6-RIME at day 2 were not encoded by significantly DEGs identified by day 2 RNA-seq (GATA6-/- vs. WT) while 18.2% were, including TLE1, VRTN, and ZIC2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that GATA6 functions in parallel with most interacting proteins identified.

claim: GATA6 functions in parallel with most interacting proteins identified by RIME.
source: 81.8% of proteins identified by GATA6-RIME at day 2 were not encoded by significantly DEGs identified by day 2 RNA-seq (GATA6-/- vs. WT) while 18.2% were, including TLE1, VRTN, and ZIC2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that GATA6 functions in parallel with most interacting proteins identified.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of RIME and RNA-seq data.

claim: Many of the significantly bound proteins were components of chromatin remodeling complexes such as members of the SWI/SNF complex and the Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase (NuRD) complex.
source: Many of the significantly bound proteins were components of chromatin remodeling complexes such as members of the SWI/SNF complex (e.g., SMARCC1, SMARCA4, and ARID1A), which functions to mobilize nucleosomes and promote DNA accessibility (Mittal and Roberts, 2020), and the Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase (NuRD) complex (e.g., KDM1A, MTA1/2/3, and GATAD2A), a chromatin remodeling complex associated with transcriptional repression (Millard et al., 2016; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5B and citations to published literature.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex functions to mobilize nucleosomes and promote DNA accessibility.
source: Many of the significantly bound proteins were components of chromatin remodeling complexes such as members of the SWI/SNF complex (e.g., SMARCC1, SMARCA4, and ARID1A), which functions to mobilize nucleosomes and promote DNA accessibility (Mittal and Roberts, 2020), and the Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase (NuRD) complex (e.g., KDM1A, MTA1/2/3, and GATAD2A), a chromatin remodeling complex associated with transcriptional repression (Millard et al., 2016; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WNT/β-catenin transcriptional regulators were identified bound to GATA6, particularly at day 2 of cardiac differentiation, including the β-catenin transcriptional co-activator EP300 and the TCF/LEF transcriptional co-repressors CTBP1/2 and TLE1.
source: Interestingly, WNT/β-catenin transcriptional regulators were identified bound to GATA6, particularly at day 2 of cardiac differentiation, including the β-catenin transcriptional co-activator EP300 (Sun et al., 2000), and the TCF/LEF transcriptional co-repressors CTBP1/2 (Valenta et al., 2003; Cuilliere-Dartigues et al., 2006) and TLE1 (Brantjes et al., 2001; Figure 5B), suggesting that GATA6 may directly modulate the transcriptional response induced by WNT signaling by binding to these proteins.
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5B and citations to published literature.

claim: GATA6 may directly modulate the transcriptional response induced by WNT signaling by binding to WNT/β-catenin transcriptional regulators.
source: Interestingly, WNT/β-catenin transcriptional regulators were identified bound to GATA6, particularly at day 2 of cardiac differentiation, including the β-catenin transcriptional co-activator EP300 (Sun et al., 2000), and the TCF/LEF transcriptional co-repressors CTBP1/2 (Valenta et al., 2003; Cuilliere-Dartigues et al., 2006) and TLE1 (Brantjes et al., 2001; Figure 5B), suggesting that GATA6 may directly modulate the transcriptional response induced by WNT signaling by binding to these proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on RIME analysis.

claim: Proteins identified by GATA6-RIME only at day 2 included the transcription factors EOMES and MIXL1 as well as TLE1, EP300, and SMARCA5.
source: Proteins identified by GATA6-RIME only at day 2 included the transcription factors EOMES and MIXL1 (both transcription factors involved in primitive streak formation and mesoderm patterning Loh et al., 2016; Stavish et al., 2020) as well at TLE1, EP300, and SMARCA5, while the unique day 4 proteins were all RNA binding proteins such as TAF15 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: EOMES and MIXL1 are both transcription factors involved in primitive streak formation and mesoderm patterning.
source: Proteins identified by GATA6-RIME only at day 2 included the transcription factors EOMES and MIXL1 (both transcription factors involved in primitive streak formation and mesoderm patterning Loh et al., 2016; Stavish et al., 2020) as well at TLE1, EP300, and SMARCA5, while the unique day 4 proteins were all RNA binding proteins such as TAF15 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The unique day 4 GATA6-RIME proteins were all RNA binding proteins such as TAF15.
source: Proteins identified by GATA6-RIME only at day 2 included the transcription factors EOMES and MIXL1 (both transcription factors involved in primitive streak formation and mesoderm patterning Loh et al., 2016; Stavish et al., 2020) as well at TLE1, EP300, and SMARCA5, while the unique day 4 proteins were all RNA binding proteins such as TAF15 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The overlapping day 2 and 4 GATA6-RIME results included many chromatin remodelers such as SMARCC1, SMARCA4, and KDM1A.

claim: The enrichment for chromatin remodelers was greater at day 2 compared to day 4.

evidence: This is supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: GATA6 immunoprecipitation on GATA6+/+ and GATA6-/- samples at day 2 confirmed a weak interaction with EOMES and SMARCC1 in the WT samples, with no observable bands in GATA6-/- samples.
source: As day 2 of differentiation had the highest level of GATA6 expression and enrichment for RIME identified proteins, we performed GATA6 immunoprecipitation (IP) on GATA6+/+ and GATA6-/- samples at day 2 and confirmed a weak interaction with EOMES and SMARCC1 in the WT samples, with no observable bands in GATA6-/- samples (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: It is possible that the interaction between GATA6 and EOMES and/or SMARCC1 is indirect.
source: The EOMES and SMARCC1 protein bands identified in GATA6-IP samples were notably less than observed for the input controls; therefore, it is possible that the interaction between GATA6 and these proteins is indirect (i.e., GATA6 may be co-bound in a complex with EOMES and/or SMARCC1 among other proteins).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the immunoprecipitation data.

claim: 26 proteins were present in all four datasets (day 2 and 4 GATA6-RIME from this study, day 4 GATA6-RIME and day 2 EOMES-RIME from published studies).
source: 26 proteins were present in all four datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), implying there is a common interaction between GATA6 and various remodeler proteins, the transcription factor SALL4, and the TCF/LEF co-repressors CTBP1/2 during mesendoderm patterning toward both cardiac mesoderm and DE lineages.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There is a common interaction between GATA6 and various remodeler proteins, the transcription factor SALL4, and the TCF/LEF co-repressors CTBP1/2 during mesendoderm patterning toward both cardiac mesoderm and DE lineages.
source: 26 proteins were present in all four datasets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C), implying there is a common interaction between GATA6 and various remodeler proteins, the transcription factor SALL4, and the TCF/LEF co-repressors CTBP1/2 during mesendoderm patterning toward both cardiac mesoderm and DE lineages.

source: Protein interactions unique to day 2 GATA6- and EOMES-RIME included MIXL1, SMARCC2, and ARID1B and may represent protein interactions specific to mesendoderm development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of RIME datasets.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The varying protein interactions between GATA6 and WNT regulators may reflect the differing contributions of the WNT pathway during cardiac and DE differentiation.
source: Cardiac differentiation requires a transient inhibition of the canonical WNT signaling pathway (Ueno et al., 2007), and as day 4 of our cardiac differentiation protocol occurs after WNT inhibition these varying protein interactions may reflect the differing contributions of the WNT pathway during cardiac and DE differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the RIME data and cited literature.

claim: LGR5 is a component of the WNT pathway.
source: LGR5, a component of the WNT pathway (de Lau et al., 2014), was among the most significant dDEGs identified from day 2 or 3 RNA-seq in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT) and was also found significantly bound by GATA6 (and in a previous study, EOMES; Teo et al., 2011) in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LGR5 was among the most significant decreased DEGs identified from day 2 or 3 RNA-seq in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT).
source: LGR5, a component of the WNT pathway (de Lau et al., 2014), was among the most significant dDEGs identified from day 2 or 3 RNA-seq in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT) and was also found significantly bound by GATA6 (and in a previous study, EOMES; Teo et al., 2011) in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: LGR5 was found significantly bound by GATA6 and EOMES in WT cells.
source: LGR5, a component of the WNT pathway (de Lau et al., 2014), was among the most significant dDEGs identified from day 2 or 3 RNA-seq in GATA6-/- cells (relative to WT) and was also found significantly bound by GATA6 (and in a previous study, EOMES; Teo et al., 2011) in WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&RUN data and a citation to published literature.

claim: LGR5 is required for efficient CM differentiation in hPSCs.
source: As LGR5 is required for efficient CM differentiation in hPSCs (Jha et al., 2017; Sahara et al., 2019), we hypothesized that infection with a doxycycline (DOX)-inducible LGR5-expressing lentivirus might rescue the cardiac defects in GATA6-/- hESCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DOX treatment of iLGR5-transduced GATA6-/- hESCs did not result in generation of beating CMs.
